title: The article that sticks to the end
goal: Use the Norwegian definite article — which doesn't stand in front of the noun but sticks to the end of it — and recognize the three noun genders along with their shortcut.
bekal: turn *en bil* into *bilen*, *ei bok* into *boka*, *et hus* into *huset*
know why you can skip *ei* almost entirely — and the seven words you can't
use *den*, *det*, *denne* and *dette* to point at things
wave: Go back over **Unit 2** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the dialogue. Notice where *ikke* goes in every negative sentence.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hvor er nøkkelen?
dialogs.intro: Early morning, and Budi is already late. Ahmad spent the night on the sofa and has only just woken up.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Ahmad! Have you seen the key?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Nøkkelen? Nei. Ligger den ikke på bordet?
lines.id: The key? No. Isn't it on the table?
lines.literal: the-key? no. lies it not on the-table?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bordet er tomt. Og stolen også.
lines.id: The table's empty. And so is the chair.
lines.literal: the-table is empty. and the-chair also.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Se i sekken. Eller i jakka.
lines.id: Look in the backpack. Or in the jacket.
lines.literal: look in the-backpack. or in the-jacket.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jakka henger ved døra… Nei, den er tom.
lines.id: The jacket's hanging by the door… No, it's empty.
lines.literal: the-jacket hangs by the-door… no, it is empty.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Hva med vinduet? Du åpnet det i går.
lines.id: What about the window? You opened it yesterday.
lines.literal: what with the-window? you opened it in yesterday.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vent… Her er den! Under avisa.
lines.id: Wait… Here it is! Under the newspaper.
lines.literal: wait… here is it! under the-newspaper.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Selvfølgelig. Det er alltid det siste stedet.
lines.id: Of course. It's always the last place.
lines.literal: of-course. it is always the last the-place.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Takk! Kan du lukke vinduet når du går?
lines.id: Thanks! Can you close the window when you leave?
lines.literal: thanks! can you close the-window when you go?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Ja ja. Og lyset og døra. Jeg kan rutinen.
lines.id: Yes, yes. And the light and the door. I know the routine.
lines.literal: yes yes. and the-light and the-door. I know the-routine.

notes: **This is the most foreign feature of Norwegian for an English ear.** There's no separate word for "the" in front of the noun. The article **sticks to the end**: *en nøkkel* (a key) → *nøkkelen* (the key). Apart from the other Scandinavian languages, hardly any major language works like this.

**The ending is exactly the same as the indefinite article, just moved.** *en* → *-en*, *ei* → *-a*, *et* → *-et*. Once you know a noun's gender, you automatically know its ending. That's why the vocabulary in this course is always given with *en/ei/et* in front.

**Spelled -et, said -e.** *Huset* is pronounced **HÜ-seh**, *bordet* **BOO-reh**, *vinduet* **VIN-dü-eh**. The *t* in this ending is almost always silent. This is one of the biggest sound traps for beginners — and it applies to the word *det* itself too, which is pronounced **deh**.

**Jakka, døra, avisa** — here's where the *-a* ending shows up. All three are feminine nouns, and the *-a* form sounds far more natural to Norwegians than *jakken*, *døren*, *avisen*, although those forms are also correct. The rules of the game are in the box on the next page.

**Den er tom** — notice *den*, not *det*. *Jakka* isn't a neuter noun, so the pronoun that replaces it is *den*. If the thing is an *et*-word, the replacement is *det*: *vinduet… det er lukket*. English has just one "it" for everything.

**Se i sekken** is an imperative, and Norwegian imperatives are always **the bare stem, with no å and no -r**: *å se* → *se!*, *å komme* → *kom!*, *å lukke* → *lukk!* The full rule is waiting in Unit 13.

grammars.title: Three genders, four forms
body: These four columns are the heart of the whole unit — and in fact the heart of the entire Norwegian noun system. Copy them into your notes and stick them somewhere you look often.
after: Read each row from left to right like a sentence: a car → the car → cars → the cars.
Words that already end in *-e* don't add another *e*: *en jente* → *jenta*, *et eple* → *eplet*. The ending attaches directly.
Words ending in *-el*, *-en*, *-er* drop the middle *e* when an ending is added: *en nøkkel* → *nøkkelen* but plural *nøkler*; *en søster* → *søsteren* → *søstre*.
One-syllable words with a single consonant after a short vowel double that consonant: *et rom* → *rommet*, *en venn* → *vennen*, *en topp* → *toppen*.

grammars.title: Good news: you can skip ei
body: Bokmål lets you treat **every** feminine noun as masculine. So *ei bok* can be written *en bok*, and *boka* can be written *boken*. Both are correct, both are used in national newspapers, and nobody will correct you.
after: **Practical advice for beginners:** use *en* for every noun that isn't *et*, and you instantly cut the genders from three to two. You'll still be right one hundred percent of the time.

⚠️ But a handful of words are **heard far more often** in their *-a* form, and you'll keep meeting them everywhere: **boka**, **jenta**, **hytta** (the cabin), **klokka** (the clock), **uka** (the week), **døra** (the door), **sola** (the sun). Learn to recognize these forms so you can **read** them, even if you choose to write *boken* yourself.
Neuter nouns (*et*) get no such freedom. *Et hus* is always *et hus* and can never become *en hus*. This is the only gender you really must learn word by word.

grammars.title: Pointing: den, det, denne, dette
body: When you really want to point at something — "**this** book", "**that** house" — Norwegian puts a demonstrative in front **and** keeps the ending.
after: Notice that the ending **stays**: *denne bok**a***, not *denne bok*. This is different from Danish and Swedish, which drop it here, so don't carry habits over from them.
*Den* and *det* also work as "it" for things — exactly like English *it*. Choose *det* if the thing is an *et*-word, *den* if not.

sections.title: Eye training: one word, four forms

blocks.text: Read this table aloud, one whole row at a time, from left to right. It's a drill that looks boring and is exactly the one that works best.

The last rows show an important habit: **one-syllable** neuter nouns don't change in the indefinite plural (*et hus → to hus*, like English *sheep*), while those with two or more syllables do take *-er* (*et vindu → to vinduer*). The full plural rules are waiting in the next unit.

sections.title: Why this feels strange to an English speaker

blocks.text: English marks definiteness with a separate word in front — *the* book, *a* book — and that habit leads to two typical mistakes:

items: **Translating "the" as a separate word.** *Den bil* for "the car" is wrong: plain "the" is the ending, *bilen*. *Den* in front only means "**that** car" — and then the ending stays too: *den bilen*.

**Dropping the ending after a demonstrative.** *Denne bok* looks logical to an English eye ("this book" has no extra "the"), but in Norwegian it's wrong — it has to be *denne boka*. The mistake is removing the ending, not keeping it.

One thing works just like English: a bare noun is fine for professions (*jeg er lærer*, though English adds "a"), languages (*jeg snakker norsk*) and fixed expressions (*på jobb*, *på skolen*, *til fots*, *i går*). Learn those expressions whole; don't take them apart.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Point at five things around you right now. Name each one in all four forms: *en stol — stolen — stoler — stolene*.
If you get stuck, it isn't because you don't know the rule — it's because you don't know the noun's gender. Always write your vocabulary with *en*/*et* in front, no exceptions.
A quick rule for when you're really stuck: about **three quarters** of Norwegian nouns are *en*-words. Guess *en* and the odds are three to one.
